options: Removes all filters from the specified table
Removes only filters on numeric columns
Creates a new calculated table
Returns the count of rows in the table
questions.explain: ALL(Table) clears every filter that was active on that table, giving an expression access to all its rows regardless of context.

questions.q: In a ratio-to-total measure like 'SUMX(ResellerSales, ...) / SUMX(ALL(ResellerSales), ...)', what role does ALL play?
options: It gives the denominator the full grand total, ignoring whatever filters are active for the numerator
It filters the numerator down to one category
It removes the relationship between two tables
It converts the measure into a calculated column
questions.explain: ALL(ResellerSales) in the denominator ensures the total always reflects every row, regardless of report filters, so dividing produces a correct percentage of the whole.

questions.q: How does ALLEXCEPT(Table, Column1) differ from ALL(Column1)?
options: ALLEXCEPT removes every filter on the table except the named column(s); ALL(Column1) removes filters from only the named column(s)
They are functionally identical in every case
ALLEXCEPT only works on numeric columns
ALL(Column1) clears the entire model's filters, while ALLEXCEPT only clears one table
questions.explain: ALLEXCEPT takes the opposite approach: name what to keep, clear everything else — useful when a table has many columns and you only want to preserve one or two.

questions.q: When is ALLEXCEPT typically the more convenient choice over ALL?
options: When a table has many columns and you only want to preserve a few, rather than listing every other column to remove
When you want to remove filters from the entire model, not just one table
When working exclusively with DirectQuery data sources
ALLEXCEPT is never more convenient than ALL
questions.explain: Choosing between ALL and ALLEXCEPT comes down to which list — columns to clear, or columns to keep — is shorter and more readable for a given table.

questions.q: What is auto-exist, and why is it worth knowing about?
options: A Power BI optimization that can affect how ALL() behaves when filtering on two or more columns of the same table
A feature that automatically creates relationships between all tables
A setting that disables all filters by default
A DAX function for detecting duplicate rows
questions.explain: Auto-exist can merge multiple same-table filters together in a way that makes ALL() not fully ignore them as expected — an edge case worth checking if an ALL()-based ratio produces unexpected numbers.
